title: Mixture-of-Experts Architecture
subtitle: Topic: Mixture-of-Experts Architecture · Subject: Neural Network Architectures · Seven levels, 28 options, seven custom diagrams and a tested PyTorch routing example.
hero:
MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS · NEURAL NETWORK ARCHITECTURES

Many experts. Selective computation.

A learned router activates a few expert subnetworks for each token, then combines their outputs.

questions.stem: What is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture in a neural network, and how do a router and multiple experts work together?
options: A Mixture-of-Experts layer contains several subnetworks and a router, but one expert is permanently assigned to all tokens in an entire training dataset. Other experts only participate during a final model-merging step.

A Mixture-of-Experts layer contains several expert subnetworks and a router that chooses which experts process each token. Selected expert outputs are combined, allowing specialized capacity without executing every available expert for each token.

A Mixture-of-Experts layer uses a router to rank its expert subnetworks, but every expert processes every token before selection. Routing changes output weights only, so sparse expert execution is not possible.

A Mixture-of-Experts layer contains expert networks chosen by a router, but expert outputs are kept as independent predictions. Their contributions are never combined into the representation passed to the next neural-network layer.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) uses several feed-forward expert networks inside a larger model. A learned router looks at a token's hidden state and selects a small subset of experts. Their results are combined and passed onward. Imagine a multilingual assistant: some experts may become better at particular language patterns, although specialization is learned rather than manually guaranteed. A single token need not run every expert. The router, selected experts, and output combination form the key idea.

questions.stem: How does sparse Mixture-of-Experts architecture differ from a dense neural-network layer, and why can it increase parameter capacity without using every expert per token?
options: A sparse MoE layer selects top-k experts, but each selected expert must execute the entire parameter bank before its output is retained. Total expert capacity grows while arithmetic per token remains proportional to every expert.

A sparse MoE layer reduces the model's stored parameters by keeping only the top-k selected experts in memory. Experts not selected for a given token are removed permanently, so total model capacity stays small.

A sparse MoE layer activates a top-k subset, but all unselected experts still execute their full feed-forward calculations for every token. This keeps processing identical to dense execution while reducing only router overhead.

A sparse MoE layer uses only a selected top-k subset of experts for each token, while a dense layer computes its entire relevant block. More total expert parameters increase capacity, but inactive experts still require storage.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A dense feed-forward block runs its weights for each token. A sparse MoE layer holds multiple expert blocks but uses only a few for any one token. For example, a router may select two of eight experts, so the token does not run all eight expert networks. This raises total parameter capacity without multiplying expert computation by eight. However, the inactive experts still occupy memory or must be stored on other devices. Routing and communication can also reduce the practical speed benefit.

questions.stem: How does top-k expert routing select and combine expert outputs, and what role do routing scores play during training?
options: A router scores the available experts for each token, selects the highest-ranked k, and combines their outputs using routing weights. Training can update selected experts and routing parameters, allowing useful specialization to emerge over time.

A router scores all experts after every expert has already processed the token, selects the highest-ranked k outputs, and combines them. Training can update the selected experts, but this ordering cannot reduce expert computation.

A router scores available experts and selects the highest-ranked k for each token, but combines their outputs with equal importance regardless of routing values. Training only adjusts the expert weights because router scores remain fixed.

A router ranks experts and chooses the highest-scoring subset, but it keeps only one expert's result and permanently disables the others for later tokens. Training therefore updates a single expert regardless of future inputs.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Top-k routing starts with a learned score for every expert, usually based on the token representation. The router picks the best k experts and uses their scores as weights when merging their outputs. For example, a token might be routed to two experts with normalized weights of 0.7 and 0.3. During training, selected experts and the router can learn from the task loss. The nonselected experts generally do not perform that token's forward expert computation.

questions.stem: What happens when an MoE router sends most tokens to only a few experts, and how do load balancing and expert capacity policies address this problem?
options: Uneven routing improves expert specialization without affecting system performance, because overloaded experts process extra tokens at the same speed. Load-balancing losses mainly adjust prediction confidence rather than distributing work across available expert devices.

Uneven routing can overload certain experts, but the standard solution is to make all experts execute every token. Capacity policies then eliminate dispatch traffic, while sparse routing and model capacity remain otherwise unchanged.

Uneven routing can overload popular experts while leaving others undertrained, causing delays and poor utilization. Load-balancing objectives encourage broader expert use, while capacity policies manage excess tokens; these choices can affect quality and communication overhead.

Uneven routing can leave some experts undertrained, but capacity limits always preserve all token computations without delay or dropping. Load-balancing objectives guarantee exactly equal traffic and cannot change model predictions or compute.
questions.explanation: Explanation: An MoE router may favor a few experts. Those experts become busy while others receive too few tokens to train well. This is called load imbalance, and extreme imbalance can resemble expert collapse. A training objective can encourage more even routing, while capacity limits or dropless dispatch policies control how excess tokens are handled. For example, a customer-service model with one crowded expert may stall despite having idle GPUs. Track token counts per expert, dropped-token rates when applicable, and task quality together.

questions.stem: How could you implement a simple top-2 Mixture-of-Experts layer in PyTorch using a learned router, expert modules, and weighted token dispatch?
options: Create expert modules and a learned router, score each token, then run every expert on all tokens before selecting two outputs. Combining those weighted outputs gives correct routing behavior but eliminates sparse computation only during training.

Create several expert modules and a learned router, compute scores per token, select two experts with topk, execute each expert on assigned tokens, and combine weighted outputs. A simple Python loop demonstrates sparse routing without optimized kernels.

Create multiple experts and a learned router, choose two scores per token, then execute only the highest-scoring single expert. Keep the second selection for logging rather than computing or combining its output.

Create expert modules and a router with topk scores, but dispatch all tokens to the same two fixed experts for the entire training run. The router's scores change weights without changing which experts process tokens.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A minimal PyTorch MoE can create several `nn.Linear` experts and one router layer. The router generates a score for each token-expert pair, `topk(2)` selects two experts, and only assigned tokens run through each expert. Their weighted contributions are accumulated into the output. For example, six tokens might be spread across four experts. The code below uses a clear Python loop instead of fast grouped kernels, so it teaches real sparse dispatch but is not a production serving implementation.

questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

Dispatch only assigned tokens

PyTorch · selective top-2 routing14 lines
01 import torch
02 from torch import nn
03 router = nn.Linear(8, 4)
04 experts = nn.ModuleList(nn.Linear(8, 8) for _ in range(4))
05 tokens = torch.randn(6, 8)
06 prob = router(tokens).softmax(-1)
07 weight, choice = prob.topk(2, dim=-1)
08 weight = weight / weight.sum(-1, keepdim=True)
09 result = torch.zeros_like(tokens)
10 for expert_id, expert in enumerate(experts):
11     row, slot = (choice == expert_id).nonzero(as_tuple=True)
12     if row.numel():
13         result.index_add_(0, row, weight[row,slot,None] * expert(tokens[row]))
14 print(result.shape)

Runs on CPU with PyTorch. Educational sparse token dispatch with router gradients; no load balancing, expert capacity control, or optimized grouped kernels.

This compact PyTorch example runs experts on selected tokens rather than on the entire batch.

questions.stem: How does expert parallelism run MoE models across multiple GPUs, and what communication, memory, and performance costs does it introduce?
options: Expert parallelism puts different experts on separate GPUs, but routes each token through every expert before receiving results. It removes load imbalance by making all experts equally busy, so communication and computation remain constant.

Expert parallelism stores a full copy of every expert on every GPU, while token batches are divided only by training example. No cross-device token dispatch is necessary, and the architecture behaves exactly like conventional data parallelism.

Expert parallelism distributes experts across GPUs and returns their outputs, but all-to-all communication occurs only when writing checkpoints. Runtime expert routing uses local memory reads, even when selected experts reside on remote devices.

Expert parallelism places different experts on different GPUs. Tokens move to devices hosting their selected experts, and their outputs return for combination. All-to-all communication, skewed expert loads, and stored parameters can limit throughput and memory efficiency.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Expert parallelism assigns experts to different devices. A router's choices determine where each token's hidden state must travel, and selected outputs are sent back for merging. For example, one GPU may host experts 1–2 and another experts 3–4; tokens choosing expert 4 must reach the second device. All-to-all token exchange, expert load imbalance, and activation buffers may become bottlenecks. Sharding experts can reduce each GPU's expert-weight memory, but system-wide memory and communication still need careful planning.

questions.stem: How should engineers evaluate and deploy a Mixture-of-Experts model while controlling routing imbalance, accuracy, memory use, throughput, and tail latency?
options: Evaluate task quality alongside active and total parameter counts, expert utilization, routing distribution, memory, throughput, and tail latency. Test realistic token mixes, verify checkpoint restoration and load-balancing behavior, and benchmark the actual serving hardware before deployment.

Evaluate an MoE primarily from total parameter count and average token accuracy, since sparse routing ensures constant compute per request. Expert utilization and tail latency need no monitoring after a successful training run.

Evaluate task quality and expert utilization on a small balanced sample, then assume identical throughput for any production request mix. Token-dispatch overhead can be inferred accurately from active parameter count without device benchmarks.

Evaluate an MoE using average latency, memory and expert counts, but ignore rarely selected experts and checkpoint routing state. If aggregate accuracy is high, uneven traffic cannot cause production bottlenecks or model recovery failures.
questions.explanation: Explanation: An MoE model can have high total capacity while activating only a fraction of its experts per token. That makes total and active parameter counts different, and neither number captures all operational costs. For example, a chat service may experience slower p95 responses when many tokens suddenly select one GPU's experts. Test realistic input distributions, expert utilization, routing stability, dropped-token policies, memory, and throughput. Verify checkpoint and router restoration, then measure actual latency and task quality on the intended serving hardware.
